key_claims: The heart ages unevenly, with inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than uniformly across the heart muscle.
Aging macrophages show increased activity in genes related to inflammation, while fibroblasts display molecular characteristics associated with fibrosis.
Certain markers associated with aging and cellular senescence were unexpectedly present in young hearts, indicating they do not reliably establish senescence on their own.

Aging produced different molecular patterns in male and female mouse hearts, with male fibroblasts showing stronger connections to fibrosis and female changes relating to development and protein production.
Some molecular aging processes observed in mice also appeared in previously published human heart data.
limitations: The findings describe molecular and cellular differences rather than demonstrated differences in heart function or disease risk.
Results regarding sex differences reflect molecular activity rather than proven variations in clinical outcomes.
Much of the cellular mapping data was derived from a mouse model, though compared against human data.
what_not_to_say: This research proves a new treatment for preventing heart aging in humans.
The discovered cellular changes directly cause heart disease or cardiac arrest.
Exercise or diet changes are proven to reverse these specific cellular pathways in people based on this study alone.
